# Multiple Solutions Side by Side

The same problem is solved two or three ways in one deliverable, and the **trade-off between them is
the point**. Distinct from [[keep-the-superseded-version-in-tree]]: there, one version is wrong or
retired; here, all of them work.

## The instances

**Oracle: three formulations per question.** Top-N is written with `ROWNUM`, with a `WITH` clause, and
with `FETCH FIRST … WITH TIES` — including a note on the `ROWNUM`-applied-before-`ORDER BY` trap.
"Empty bands" is written as a `LEFT JOIN` anti-join, as `MINUS`, and as `NOT EXISTS`. Chain-of-chiefs
is written three ways over the self-referencing hierarchy. One rule is implemented twice as a trigger,
with the inferior version labelled — see [[database-triggers]].

> "The branches are disjoint by construction, so UNION ALL is used instead of UNION: there are no
> duplicates for UNION to remove, and skipping the sort and de-duplication pass is free."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/sql/02_queries/03_joins_and_sets.sql, 2026-07-25

**Python labs: a deliberate CLI A/B.** Lab 09 ships `click` while the core package ships `argparse`,
on comparable problems, and says why:

> "**`click` against `argparse`.** This lab uses `click`; the core CLI in `weblog.cli` uses
> `argparse`. Comparing the two on the same kind of problem is the point — `click`'s decorators are
> terser for flag soup, `argparse`'s subparsers give more control over a command hierarchy."
> — Python-Programming-Laboratories/labs/09_dataset_reports/README.md, 2026-07-25

See [[click-versus-argparse]]. The same repo keeps a hand-written "teaching version" of a parser
beside the production one, for the same reason — see [[keep-the-teaching-version]].

**Warehouse: a second implementation as the specification.** `rsi_reference.py` computes the RSI in
Python over SQLite specifically because SQLite's window syntax matches T-SQL's, making it a portable
cross-check on the warehouse implementation. See
{{reference-implementation-as-specification}}. The wiki records one caveat: the script only *prints*,
so the two-implementation diff was never actually asserted.

**Discrete maths: the same system in two stacks.** Lab 6 exists as Cypher against Neo4j and as an
offline JS viewer that reimplements every query, rendering the graph beside the Cypher that produces
it. Lab 4 exists in Python and in the browser. See [[dual-implementation-as-cross-check]].

**Optimisation: five algorithms on one benchmark.** Greedy, Random Search, GA, Tabu Search and
Iterated Local Search all race on the same six Taillard instances with a shared evaluator and a shared
CSV contract, so the convergence plots are directly comparable. See
{{permutation-flow-shop-scheduling}} and [[iterated-local-search]].

## What it is for

Two things, and they are different:

1. **Teaching a trade-off.** The Oracle and Python cases exist to show that a choice was available.
2. **Cross-checking a result.** The RSI and Neo4j cases exist so that two independent paths must agree
   — a cheap substitute for a test suite in repos that have none. This is the same motive as
   [[generated-audit-artifact]], reached without any tooling.

## Cost

Duplication drifts. `Discrete-Mathematics-Laboratories` had to correct a count from 38 objects to 39
"throughout" after its guide and README disagreed, and its `guide.txt` checklist still says 38 — see
[[documentation-drift]]. Two implementations mean two things to keep true.
